Zooplankton are tiny animals (and animal-like organisms) that live in water and drift with currents rather than swimming on their own. They are one of the most important groups of living things on Earth.

The word "zooplankton" describes a category of living things, not a single species. It covers a huge variety of organisms that share two key traits:

  1. They are animals or animal-like — meaning they cannot make their own food from sunlight. They must eat other things to survive.
  2. They drift — they live in water (oceans, lakes, rivers, ponds) and are carried by currents. Some can swim a little, but not strongly enough to fight a current.

Zooplankton range dramatically in size. Most are microscopic — invisible without a magnifying glass or microscope. But some, like jellyfish, are large enough to see easily with the naked eye.
Where do they fit in the bigger picture?

To understand zooplankton well, you need to understand the word plankton first.

Plankton is the collective name for all the tiny drifting life in water — anything too small or too weak to swim against currents. Plankton splits into two big groups:

  • Phytoplankton — the "plant" side. These are microscopic, plant-like organisms (mostly algae and cyanobacteria) that make their own food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide — exactly like plants on land do. They are the primary producers of the water world.
  • Zooplankton — the "animal" side. These are organisms that must eat to get energy. They cannot make food themselves.

So zooplankton is simply the animal half of plankton.
What kinds of organisms are zooplankton?

The variety is remarkable:

  • Tiny crustaceans like copepods and krill. Copepods are arguably the most numerous multi-celled animals on Earth. Krill are slightly larger (a few centimetres), shrimp-like creatures that exist in such enormous numbers in Antarctic waters that they can turn the sea red.
  • Single-celled organisms like foraminifera and radiolarians — microscopic creatures with beautiful, intricate shells.
  • Larvae of larger animals — baby crabs, baby fish, baby worms, and baby sea urchins all start life as zooplankton before growing up and settling into their adult forms. This is sometimes called meroplankton (temporary plankton).
  • Jellyfish — yes, jellyfish are classified as zooplankton because they mostly drift rather than swim purposefully.
  • Arrow worms, pteropods (tiny sea snails), and many other small ocean creatures.

Most zooplankton eat phytoplankton — the microscopic plant-like organisms mentioned earlier. Some eat bacteria. Some eat other zooplankton smaller than themselves. A few feed on tiny bits of dead, sinking organic matter. The key point is that they are all consumers — they gain energy by eating, not by photosynthesising.

Almost everything bigger than them. Small fish eat zooplankton. Larger fish eat the small fish. Even some of the largest animals on Earth — blue whales and whale sharks — feed almost entirely on zooplankton (especially krill), filtering enormous quantities of water to collect them.

This makes zooplankton the critical link between the microscopic plant world and the visible animal world. Without them, the energy locked in phytoplankton could not reach fish, whales, seabirds, or the seafood on your plate.

1. They are the foundation of aquatic food webs.
Every fish in the ocean — and therefore most of the seafood humans eat — depends either directly or indirectly on zooplankton. If zooplankton disappeared, ocean food chains would collapse within a very short time.

2. They help regulate Earth's climate.
When zooplankton eat phytoplankton, and then die or produce waste, their remains sink toward the ocean floor, carrying carbon with them. This process — called the biological pump — transfers enormous amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere into the deep ocean, where it is stored for centuries or longer. Zooplankton are therefore a crucial natural mechanism that slows climate change.

3. They produce oxygen — indirectly.
Phytoplankton produce roughly half of all the oxygen on Earth (more than all the rainforests combined). Zooplankton help keep phytoplankton populations healthy and balanced by grazing on them — preventing any one species from growing out of control and crashing. A healthy zooplankton population means a healthy phytoplankton population, which means more oxygen.

4. They are indicators of ecosystem health.
Scientists monitor zooplankton populations closely. When the numbers or types of zooplankton in a body of water change, it often signals bigger problems — pollution, warming water temperatures, ocean acidification, or ecosystem disruption.

• Zooplankton works as both a singular noun and a plural noun. You can say "a zooplankton" (referring to one organism) or "zooplankton are declining in the North Atlantic" (referring to the group as a whole). In scientific writing, both are common.
  • It is used in biology, ecology, oceanography, environmental science, and climate science.
  • "Marine zooplankton" specifies ocean-dwelling ones. "Freshwater zooplankton" refers to those in lakes and rivers. Without a modifier, the word most commonly refers to ocean-dwelling zooplankton.

Zooplankton are drifting, animal-type organisms in water — ranging from microscopic single-celled creatures to jellyfish — that eat phytoplankton and other small life, feed nearly everything bigger than themselves, and quietly keep the planet's oceans, climate, and oxygen supply functioning.
